title: Tunable non-Hermitian skin effect and topological phases in ladders with staggered nonreciprocal inter-leg hopping
abstract: We investigate the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) and topological phases in a ladder model with staggered nonreciprocal inter-leg hopping, consisting of an Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain coupled to a normal tight-binding chain. By tuning the system parameters, we show that the direction of the NHSE under open boundary conditions can be reversed and can even become energy dependent. The NHSE is further characterized by the spectral winding number under periodic boundary conditions. We further demonstrate that the inter-leg coupling significantly enlarges the topologically nontrivial parameter regime. Remarkably, the zero-energy topological edge modes reside on different legs of the ladder and are characterized by real-space winding numbers $W=\pm1$. Furthermore, increasing the nonreciprocity of the inter-leg hopping modifies the topological phase boundaries and eventually drives the system into a topologically trivial phase. Our results establish staggered nonreciprocal inter-leg hopping as an effective mechanism for engineering both the non-Hermitian skin effect and topological phases in ladder systems.
summary: This work explores a ladder model featuring staggered, nonreciprocal inter-leg hopping to study its impact on non-Hermiticity and topology. The authors show that this specific coupling mechanism allows for the precise tuning of the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect direction and magnitude. Crucially, they map out parameter regimes where robust topological edge modes exist, demonstrating a powerful tool for engineering quantum states in quasi-1D systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how staggered nonreciprocal inter-leg hopping influences both the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) and topological phases in a ladder lattice.
main_result: The research demonstrates that this specific coupling mechanism allows for engineering tunable NHSE, enabling its reversal and energy dependence. Furthermore, it establishes a clear link between nonreciprocity and topology, showing how the system can transition into trivial phases by tuning parameters.
method: The analysis employs theoretical diagonalization of the Hamiltonian under both open and periodic boundary conditions, utilizing diagnostics like the directional Inverse Participation Ratio (dIPR) and spectral/real-space winding numbers.
model_or_system: The system is a ladder model composed of an Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain coupled to a uniform tight-binding chain via staggered nonreciprocal inter-leg hopping. The Hamiltonian incorporates parameters controlling the SSH hopping ($v$) and the nonreciprocity ($\gamma$).
key_observables: Directional Inverse Participation Ratio (dIPR), spectral winding number, real-space winding numbers ($W=\pm1$), zero-energy topological edge modes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system can be modeled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian and that parameters are real. A limitation noted is potential ambiguity near phase boundaries due to finite precision.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate eigenstate localization (dIPR) for varying $v$, compare OBC vs PBC spectra using winding numbers, and present phase diagrams mapping topological regimes ($W=\pm1$) in the $v-\gamma$ plane.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the model by first establishing the role of nonreciprocity in inducing NHSE. It then explores how tuning parameters like $v$ controls the direction and energy dependence of the skin effect, culminating in a phase diagram that maps out topologically nontrivial regimes controlled by $\gamma$.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer topological phases and control boundary localization using non-Hermitian terms via structural hopping is highly relevant for designing synthetic quantum materials or optical lattices where directional coupling can be precisely tuned.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (Color online) Schematic illustration of the ladder model. The upper leg is an SSH chain with alternating hop- ping amplitudes v and w, while the lower leg is a uniform tight-binding chain with hopping amplitude t. The inter-leg hopping is nonreciprocal, with amplitudes Jeγ and Je−γ, and alternates between odd and even sites in the two chains.

FIG. 2. (Color online) Energy spectra of the ladder model un- der open boundary conditions. Panels (a) and (b) show the real and imaginary parts of the eigenenergies, respectively, as functions of v for γ = −0.5. The color scale represents the dIPR of the corresponding eigenstates. Positive (nega- tive) dIPR values indicate states localized at the right (left) boundary of the ladder, whereas dIPR ≈0 corresponds to ex- tended states. Panels (c) and (d) show the real and imaginary parts of the eigenenergies, respectively, as functions of γ for v = 1.5. Other parameters are w = t = J = 1 and L = 100.

FIG. 3. (Color online) Spatial distributions of the eigenstates in the ladder model for different values of v: (a) v = −1.5, (b) v = −1.0, (c) v = −0.5, (d) v = 0.5, (e) v = 1.0, and (f) v = 1.5, with γ = −0.5. The eigenstates are ordered according to the real parts of the corresponding eigenenergies. The color scale represents the amplitude |ψ| of the eigenstates. The site indices 1 ≤j ≤100 correspond to the upper leg of the ladder, whereas 101 ≤j ≤200 correspond to the lower leg. Other parameters are w = t = J = 1.

FIG. 4. (Color online) Energy spectra of the ladder model under open boundary conditions (OBCs, colored dots) and periodic boundary conditions (PBCs, black dots) for γ = −0.5 and different values of v: (a) v = −1.5, (b) v = −1.0, (c) v = −0.5, (d) v = 0.5, (e) v = 1.0, and (f) v = 1.5. The color scale represents the dIPR of the OBC eigenstates. The labels Wk = ±1 denote the spectral winding numbers of the corresponding PBC spectra, which determine the direction of the NHSE under OBCs. Other parameters are the same as those in Fig. 3.

Figure 4 compares the energy spectra under OBCs and PBCs for the ladder model with v varying from −1.5 to 1.5, while the other parameters are the same as those in Fig. 3. As shown in Fig. 4, the OBC spectrum is enclosed by the corresponding PBC spectrum except at the crit- ical points v = ±1 [Figs. 4(b) and 4(e)]. At these two critical points, the OBC and PBC spectra coincide and form open arcs rather than closed loops in the complex- energy plane. Consequently, the NHSE is absent under OBCs, consistent with the extended eigenstates shown in Figs. 3(b) and 3(e).
